name: Bafia (Rigama)
place: 3rd-degree chiefdom of Rigama, Ngam canton (Mbam-et-Inoubou, Centre)
overview: In the majority in their canton, the Bafia of Rigama live alongside Bamiléké, Tikar, Hausa and Yambassa in a spirit of living together. Descended from Bakoa (Bokito), they descend from Meden to Ngam, “son of Ngam”. Farmers, basket-makers and sculptors, they dance the dom at the funerals of elders and exhibit their art at the Mbam Art festival.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority group living on good terms with the Bamiléké, Tikar, Hausa and Yambassa.
The Bafia language is spoken wherever a Bafia community lives, even in the North.
People marry freely, but not within certain large families: a migama girl and boy cannot marry each other.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: Ancestral land: the founder Meden at Ngam, a rich man, bought it from the Korro canton; adopted by Ngam, he made Rigama the “last son” of the Ngam canton.
The group comes from Bakoa (Bokito subdivision), from the family of Boya Nkono, with whom ties have remained alive.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Society now follows the administrative organisation; the chief decides with the inhabitants, natives and non-natives alike, for the common good.
Every opinion counts, and the council of women is now listened to.
The Ngam and Korro cantons are distinct: one does not inherit a chiefdom from the other canton.
Very friendly relations with the neighbours; conflicts are settled by dialogue.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the woman joins her husband's family.
Marriage is now a free union: one marries whom one loves.
People marry when they are mature; a young girl is judged ready when she can feed her father and help her brothers.
Steps: meeting of the families, “knocking at the door”, bride price, traditional marriage.
The bride price shows the woman's worth: palm wine (sign of acceptance), kola (tradition), a goat and a list of goods requested by the family.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: At the end of the year, people pray for the rest of the ancestor and the grandparents; the chiefdom is the symbolic place.
The child is a gift from God; the reincarnation of a patriarch is recognised when the child resembles him, and the child is given his name. Death is the natural end of existence, not a curse.

Taboos: the tortoise, a sacred animal used for healing, is not eaten; incest requires a purification rite. Women do not enter the sacred forest; certain animals are forbidden to children until adulthood.
Breaking the taboos would expose one to leprosy.
The ancestors consulted oracles; today, people pray according to their religion (Islam, Christianity).

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Farming, for men and women alike.
The land falls under the State, which recognises the priority of the customary guardians.
Crafts: rattan, furniture, statuettes, sold notably during the Mbam Art festival.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: The obom, a bark garment reserved for patriarchs, is worn for the needs of tradition; women wear the wrapper.
Traditional practitioners are trusted, but not marabouts.
Beauty: the responsible man who takes care of his children and is comfortable in his own skin; the woman who takes care of her family.
Courtship: good dancer, good hunter, sculptor; the hard-working woman.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: The dom, a funeral dance with the balafon, honours the death of a patriarch or matriarch; the ntapke, a festive dance, enlivens weddings.
The former community festivals have disappeared.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: Some of the Bafia have adopted Islam.

sections.title: The names
items: The birth of twins is marked by a ceremony; they are called Moudio (“the one from the sky”) and Baran.
The parents choose the name by mutual agreement; the mother of twins takes a new name, Guebediang.
The founding ancestor, Meden à Ngam, is the “son of Ngam”.

lessons.title: Who are the Bafia (Rigama)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Bafia (Rigama) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition

vocabulary.frenchText: The little snails The river of snails

lessons.competence: Introduce the Bafia (Rigama) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Bafia (Rigama) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Bafia (Rigama) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Bafia (Rigama) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Bafia (Rigama) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Majority group living on good terms with the Bamiléké, Tikar, Haoussa and Yambassa. • The Bafia language is spoken wherever a Bafia community lives, as far as the North. • People marry freely, but not within certain large families: a migama girl and boy cannot marry each other. • Ancestral land: the founder Meden at Ngam, a wealthy man, bought it from the Korro canton; adopted by Ngam, he made Rigama the “last son” of the Ngam canton. • The group comes from Bakoa (Bokito arrondissement), from the family of Boya Nkono, with which ties have remained alive.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: In the majority in their canton, the Bafia of Rigama live alongside Bamiléké, Tikar, Hausa and Yambassa in a spirit of living together. Descended from Bakoa (Bokito), they descend from Meden to Ngam, “son of Ngam”. Farmers, basket-makers and sculptors, they dance the dom at the funerals of elders and exhibit their art at the Mbam Art festival.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Bafia (Rigama) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Bafia (Rigama)
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Bafia (Rigama) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Bafia (Rigama) village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe how the Bafia (Rigama) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Bafia (Rigama) village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Society now follows the administrative organisation; the chief decides with the inhabitants, natives and non-natives alike, for the common good. steps.title: Remediation (5 min)

lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Bafia (Rigama)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Bafia (Rigama), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Bafia (Rigama).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Bafia (Rigama), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Bafia (Rigama).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: couscous and greens, tubers. • Drinks: ruwat (maize wine), palm wine. • Farming, for men and women alike.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Bafia (Rigama) eat mainly couscous and vegetables, tubers. Traditional drinks: ruwat, palm wine. These foods are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Bafia (Rigama): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Which dances are practised, and on what occasions? — Who dances (men, women, children, initiates)? When and where? — Which instruments, songs and outfits are used? — What is the cultural meaning of the chosen dance?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The dom, a funeral dance with the balafon, honours the death of a patriarch or matriarch; the ntapke, a festive dance, enlivens weddings. • The former community festivals have disappeared.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Among the Bafia (Rigama), traditional dances (funerals of elders, ntapke) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: balafon. Festival(s): Mbam Art festival.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Describe a Bafia (Rigama) dance (participants, time, instruments, gestures, meaning), then perform it with your group.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.memo: Among the Bafia (Rigama), traditional dances (funerals of elders, ntapke) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: balafon. Festival(s): Mbam Art festival.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Bafia (Rigama)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Bafia (Rigama), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Bafia (Rigama). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Bafia (Rigama), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Bafia (Rigama). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following elements: • Farming, for men and women alike. • The land belongs to the State, which recognises the priority of the customary guardians. • Crafts: rattan, furniture, statuettes, sold notably during the Mbam Art festival.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Farming, for men and women alike. The land belongs to the State, which recognises the priority of the customary guardians.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Bafia (Rigama)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Bafia (Rigama)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Bafia (Rigama), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Bafia (Rigama). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Bafia (Rigama), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Bafia (Rigama). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Prayers are said, at the end of the year, for the rest of the ancestor and the grandparents; the chiefdom is the symbolic place. • The child is a gift from God; the reincarnation of a patriarch is recognised when the child resembles him, and his name is given to the child. Death is the natural end of existence, not a curse. • Taboos: the tortoise, a sacred animal used for healing, is not eaten; incest requires a purification rite. Women do not enter the sacred forest; certain animals are forbidden to children until adulthood. • Breaking the prohibitions would expose one to leprosy. • The ancestors consulted oracles; today, people pray according to their religion (Islam, Christianity).

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: At the end of the year, people pray for the rest of the ancestor and the grandparents; the chiefdom is the symbolic place. The child is a gift from God; the reincarnation of a patriarch is recognised when the child resembles him, and the child is given his name. Death is the natural end of existence, not a curse.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Bafia (Rigama) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Rikpa'
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Bafia (Rigama) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Bafia (Rigama) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Bafia (Rigama) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Bafia (Rigama) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • The community's language is Rikpa'. • Greetings: Biayembè = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Wayembè / ntok si yo éh = morning greeting (one person); Ntok si yéh = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Bo, Bè, Ra, Ni, Tan. • The founding ancestor, Meden à Ngam, is the “son of Ngam”. • Some of the Bafia have adopted Islam.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Rikpa' are the first steps towards communicating with the Bafia (Rigama). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Rikpa'.

activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Rikpa' are the first steps towards communicating with the Bafia (Rigama). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
